questions.stem_markdown: A 17-year-old says he only drinks on some weekends but often uses cannabis later in the same session because it helps him "balance out" the alcohol. Which response is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Using cannabis after alcohol usually lowers overall adolescent substance-related risk.
This is mainly relevant if he has had a blackout; otherwise the cannabis history can be left aside.
In adolescents, mixing alcohol with other substances is a concerning drinking pattern associated with harms, so follow-up should address both substances.
Weekend-only use rules out alcohol-related dependence or withdrawal concerns.
Because cannabis is illicit, the alcohol history becomes less important.

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes state that adolescents are more likely to binge drink, be alcohol dependent, have withdrawal, **mix alcohol with other substances**, and suffer harms. A young person describing combined alcohol and cannabis use should therefore not be reassured simply because the pattern is intermittent or framed as a way to "balance out" alcohol.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes do not support the idea that adding cannabis makes adolescent drinking safer; mixing substances is itself listed as a concerning pattern.
why_others_wrong.B: The combined use remains relevant even without a blackout, because the notes identify mixing alcohol with other substances as part of risky adolescent alcohol use.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes do not say weekend-only use rules out dependence or withdrawal concerns.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes support addressing the full pattern of alcohol and other drug use rather than treating one substance as making the other irrelevant.

key_takeaways: Mixing alcohol with other substances is a note-supported adolescent risk pattern.
Intermittent use does not make combined alcohol and cannabis use reassuring.
Follow-up should address both substances and related harms.

questions.stem_markdown: During a teaching session, an intern says adolescent alcohol and other drug review can probably be de-emphasised because tobacco smoking and the use of alcohol and illicit drugs are declining overall. Which reply is **best supported** by the notes?

options.text: Declining use means substance use is no longer a major contributor to adolescent ill health.
It still matters: in 2015, alcohol and illicit drug use were the leading cause of total burden of disease in males aged 15-24 and the second and third leading causes for females.
Substance-use review is mainly needed only for males, because females have little measurable burden.
Routine review should now focus almost entirely on e-cigarettes, because alcohol and illicit drugs no longer contribute much.
Substance-use review is best reserved for adolescents who have already had a hospital presentation.

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes explicitly state that in 2015, alcohol and illicit drug use were the **leading cause of total burden of disease** in males aged 15-24 and the second and third leading causes for females. They also note that males experience nearly twice the burden of disease compared with females. So declining trends in some substances do not justify de-emphasising adolescent alcohol and other drug review.

why_others_wrong.A: This ignores the note-based burden-of-disease data showing alcohol and illicit drugs remain major contributors to harm.
why_others_wrong.C: Females are also described as having major burden from alcohol and illicit drug use, even if the burden is higher in males.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes identify e-cigarettes as a concern, but they do not support dismissing alcohol and illicit drugs as unimportant.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes support routine adolescent assessment and brief intervention, not waiting until a hospital presentation occurs.

key_takeaways: Declining prevalence does not mean substance use has become unimportant.
Alcohol and illicit drugs remain major contributors to burden of disease in young people.
Routine adolescent review should still include alcohol and other drug assessment.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old who uses cannabis regularly says, "It might make people feel weird on the night, but it doesn't cause real longer-term mental health problems." Which response is **most appropriate**?

options.text: The main ongoing concern with cannabis is appetite change rather than mental health.
Mental health follow-up is only needed if there has already been an acute panic attack.
Early-onset cannabis use is linked to anxiety, depression and psychosis, so longer-term mental health effects should still be discussed.
Cannabis-related mental health risk only matters during withdrawal.
If he is still attending school, longer-term harms are unlikely.

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes state that **early-onset cannabis** use increases the risk of anxiety, depression and psychosis. The best response is therefore to address longer-term mental health risk rather than limiting counselling to acute intoxication effects or withdrawal.

why_others_wrong.A: This minimises the note-based mental health risks linked to early cannabis use.
why_others_wrong.B: The notes do not require a prior acute panic episode before mental health risk becomes relevant.
why_others_wrong.D: Withdrawal is a separate issue; the notes specifically link early cannabis use to longer-term mental health harms as well.
why_others_wrong.E: Continued school attendance does not exclude the mental health risks described in the notes.

key_takeaways: Early-onset cannabis use is linked to anxiety, depression and psychosis.
Cannabis counselling should include longer-term mental health risk, not just acute effects.
Mental health follow-up is still relevant even without dramatic intoxication or withdrawal features.
